entries.29d30d00067ef1efd794c9f174d6d2afc1cc7937: <div sID="gen18163" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="49" osisID="Jer.49" sID="Jer.49"/> <div eID="gen18163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18164" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18165" type="x-p"/> The cup of trembling still goes round, and the nations must all drink of it, according to the instructions given to Jeremiah, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.15">ch. xxv. 15</reference>. This chapter puts it into the hands, I. Of the Ammonites, <reference osisRef="Jer.49.1-Jer.49.6">ver. 1-6</reference>. II. Of the Edomites, <reference osisRef="Jer.49.7-Jer.49.22">ver. 7-22</reference>. III. Of the Syrians, <reference osisRef="Jer.49.23-Jer.49.27">ver. 23-27</reference>. IV. Of the Kedarenes, and the kingdoms of Hazor, <reference osisRef="Jer.49.28-Jer.49.33">ver. 28-33</reference>. V. Of the Elamites, <reference osisRef="Jer.49.34-Jer.49.39">ver. 34-39</reference>. When Israel was scarcely saved where shall all these appear?
entries.36b3d872392ac5023cfbf7c283e791a3f47adc29: <div eID="gen18165" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18164" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Judgment of Ammonites. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 595.)</title> <div sID="gen18166" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Concerning the Ammonites, thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; Hath Israel no sons? hath he no heir? why <hi type="italic">then</hi> doth their king inherit Gad, and his people dwell in his cities? <hi type="super">2</hi> Therefore, behold, the days come, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , that I will cause an alarm of war to be heard in Rabbah of the Ammonites; and it shall be a desolate heap, and her daughters shall be burned with fire: then shall Israel be heir unto them that were his heirs, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">3</hi> Howl, O Heshbon, for Ai is spoiled: cry, ye daughters of Rabbah, gird you with sackcloth; lament, and run to and fro by the hedges; for their king shall go into captivity, <hi type="italic">and</hi> his priests and his princes together. <hi type="super">4</hi> Wherefore gloriest thou in the valleys, thy flowing valley, O backsliding daughter? that trusted in her treasures, <hi type="italic">saying,</hi> Who shall come unto me? <hi type="super">5</hi> Behold, I will bring a fear upon thee, saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> of hosts, from all those that be about thee; and ye shall be driven out every man right forth; and none shall gather up him that wandereth. <hi type="super">6</hi> And afterward I will bring again the captivity of the children of Ammon, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen18166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18167" type="x-p"/> The Ammonites were next, both in kindred and neighbourhood, to the Moabites, and therefore are next set to the bar. Their country joined to that of the two tribes and a half, on the other side Jordan, and was but a bad neighbour; however, being a neighbour, they shall have a share in these circular predictions. 1. An action is here brought, in God's name, against the Ammonites, for an illegal encroachment upon the rightful possessions of the tribe of Gad, that lay next them, <reference osisRef="Jer.49.1">v. 1</reference>. A writ of enquiry is brought to discover what title they had to those territories, which, upon the carrying away of the Gileadites, by the king of Assyria (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.29">2 Kings xv. 29</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.5.26">1 Chron. v. 26</reference>), were left almost dispeopled, at least unguarded, and an easy prey to the next invader. "What! Does it escheat <hi type="italic">ob defectum sanguinis—for what of an heir? Hath Israel no sons? Hath he no heir?</hi> Are there no Gadites left, to whom the right of inheritance belongs? Or, if there were not, are there no Israelites, none left of Judah, that are nearer akin to them than you are?" <hi type="italic">Why then does their king,</hi> as if he were entitled to the forfeited estates, or Milcom, their idol, as if he had the right to dispose of it to his worshippers, <hi type="italic">inherit Gad, and his people dwell in the cities</hi> which fell by lot to that tribe of God's people. Nay, there were sons and heirs of their own body, <hi type="italic">en ventre de sa mere</hi>—<hi type="italic">in their mother's womb,</hi> and the Ammonites, to prevent their claim, most barbarously murdered them (<reference osisRef="Amos.1.13">Amos i. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">They ripped up the women with child of Gilead, that they might enlarge their border,</hi> that, having seized it, none might rise up hereafter to recover it from them. Thus <hi type="italic">they magnified themselves against their border</hi> and boasted it was their own, <reference osisRef="Zeph.2.8">Zeph. ii. 8</reference>. Note, Though among men might often prevails against right, yet that might shall be controlled by the Almighty, who <hi type="italic">sits in the throne, judging right;</hi> and those will find themselves mistaken who think every thing their own which they can lay their hands on, or which none yet appears to lay claim to. As there is justice owing to owners, so also to their heirs, when they are dead, whom it is a great sin to defraud, though they either know not their right or know not how to come at it. This shall be reckoned for particularly, when injuries of this kind are done to God's people. 2. Judgment is here given against them for this violence. (1.) Terrors shall come upon them: God <hi type="italic">will cause an alarm of war to be heard,</hi> even <hi type="italic">in Rabbah,</hi> their capital city and a very strong one, <reference osisRef="Jer.49.1">v. 1</reference>. <hi type="italic">The Lord God of hosts,</hi> who has all armies at his command, <hi type="italic">will bring a fear upon them from all that be about them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.49.5">v. 5</reference>. Note, God has many ways to terrify those who have been a terror to his people. (2.) Their cities shall be laid in ruins: <hi type="italic">Rabbah,</hi> the mother-city, <hi type="italic">shall be a desolate heap, and her daughters,</hi> the other cities that have a dependence upon her, and receive law from her as daughters, <hi type="italic">shall be burnt with fire;</hi> so that the inhabitants shall be forced to quit them, and they shall <hi type="italic">cry,</hi> and <hi type="italic">gird themselves with sackcloth,</hi> as having lost all they had, and not knowing whither to betake themselves. (3.) Their country, which they were so proud of, shall be wasted (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">Wherefore gloriest thou in the valleys,</hi> and <hi type="italic">trustest in thy treasures, O backsliding daughter?</hi> They are charged with backsliding or turning away from God and from his worship, for they were the posterity of righteous Lot. It is true, they had never been so in covenant with God as Israel was; yet all idolaters may be called <hi type="italic">backsliders,</hi> for the worship of the true God was prior to that of false gods. <hi type="italic">They were untoward and refractory</hi> (so some read it); and, when they had forsaken their God, <hi type="italic">they gloried in their valleys,</hi> particularly one that was called <hi type="italic">the flowing valley,</hi> because it flowed with all good things. These they had violently taken away from Israel, and gloried in it when they had done so. They gloried in the strength of their valleys, so surrounded with mountains that they were inaccessible, gloried in the products of them, gloried <hi type="italic">in the treasures</hi> they got together out of them, <hi type="italic">saying, Who shall come unto me?</hi> While they bathed themselves in the pleasures of their country, they flattered themselves with a conceit that they should never be disturbed in the enjoyment of them: <hi type="italic">To-morrow shall be as this day;</hi> therefore they set God and his judgments at defiance; they are proud, voluptuous, and secure; but wherefore dost thou do so: Note, Those who backslide and turn away from God have little reason either to take complacency or to put confidence in any worldly enjoyments whatsoever, <reference osisRef="Hos.9.1">Hos. ix. 1</reference>. (4.) Their people, from the least to the greatest, shall be forced out of the country. Some shall flee to seek for shelter, others shall be carried into captivity, so that their land shall be quite evacuated: <hi type="italic">Their king and his princes,</hi> nay, and Milcom, their god, <hi type="italic">and his priests, shall go into captivity</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.3">v. 3</reference>), <hi type="italic">and every man shall be driven out right forth,</hi> shall take the next way, and make the best of it in his flight (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.5">v. 5</reference>), forgetting the <hi type="italic">valleys, the flowing valleys,</hi> which now fail them. And, to complete their misery, <hi type="italic">none shall gather up him that wanders,</hi> none shall open their doors to them, as Jael to Sisera, to entertain them; and those that flee shall be so much in care to secure themselves that they shall not take notice of others, no, not of those that are nearest to them, that wander, and are at a loss which way to go, as <reference osisRef="Jer.47.3">ch. xlvii. 3</reference>. (5.) Then the country of the Ammonites shall fall into the hands of the remaining Israelites (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">Then shall Israel be heir to those that were his heirs,</hi> shall possess himself of their land who had possessed themselves of his, by way of reprisal. Note, The equity of divine Providence is to be acknowledged when the losses of the injured are recompensed out of the unjust gains of the injurious. Though the enemies of God's Israel may make a prey of them for a while, the tables will shortly be turned. 3. Yet there is a prospect given them of mercy hereafter (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.6">v. 6</reference>), as before to Moab. The day will come when <hi type="italic">the captivity of the children of Ammon will</hi> be <hi type="italic">brought again;</hi> for so it is in human affairs: the wheel goes round.
entries.95d2a9ed16fb2926efef2bd302c0f6844c16439f: <div eID="gen18167" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Judgment of Edom. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 595.)</title> <div sID="gen18168" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> Concerning Edom, thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts; <hi type="italic">Is</hi> wisdom no more in Teman? is counsel perished from the prudent? is their wisdom vanished? <hi type="super">8</hi> Flee ye, turn back, dwell deep, O inhabitants of Dedan; for I will bring the calamity of Esau upon him, the time <hi type="italic">that</hi> I will visit him. <hi type="super">9</hi> If grape-gatherers come to thee, would they not leave <hi type="italic">some</hi> gleaning grapes? if thieves by night, they will destroy till they have enough. <hi type="super">10</hi> But I have made Esau bare, I have uncovered his secret places, and he shall not be able to hide himself: his seed is spoiled, and his brethren, and his neighbours, and he <hi type="italic">is</hi> not. <hi type="super">11</hi> Leave thy fatherless children, I will preserve <hi type="italic">them</hi> alive; and let thy widows trust in me. <hi type="super">12</hi> For thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; Behold, they whose judgment <hi type="italic">was</hi> not to drink of the cup have assuredly drunken; and <hi type="italic">art</hi> thou he <hi type="italic">that</hi> shall altogether go unpunished? thou shalt not go unpunished, but thou shalt surely drink <hi type="italic">of it.</hi> <hi type="super">13</hi> For I have sworn by myself, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , that Bozrah shall become a desolation, a reproach, a waste, and a curse; and all the cities thereof shall be perpetual wastes. <hi type="super">14</hi> I have heard a rumour from the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and an ambassador is sent unto the heathen, <hi type="italic">saying,</hi> Gather ye together, and come against her, and rise up to the battle. <hi type="super">15</hi> For, lo, I will make thee small among the heathen, <hi type="italic">and</hi> despised among men. <hi type="super">16</hi> Thy terribleness hath deceived thee, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the pride of thine heart, O thou that dwellest in the clefts of the rock, that holdest the height of the hill: though thou shouldest make thy nest as high as the eagle, I will bring thee down from thence, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">17</hi> Also Edom shall be a desolation: every one that goeth by it shall be astonished, and shall hiss at all the plagues thereof. <hi type="super">18</hi> As in the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah and the neighbour <hi type="italic">cities</hi> thereof, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , no man shall abide there, neither shall a son of man dwell in it. <hi type="super">19</hi> Behold, he shall come up like a lion from the swelling of Jordan against the habitation of the strong: but I will suddenly make him run away from her: and who <hi type="italic">is</hi> a chosen <hi type="italic">man, that</hi> I may appoint over her? for who <hi type="italic">is</hi> like me? and who will appoint me the time? and who <hi type="italic">is</hi> that shepherd that will stand before me? <hi type="super">20</hi> Therefore hear the counsel of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , that he hath taken against Edom; and his purposes, that he hath purposed against the inhabitants of Teman: Surely the least of the flock shall draw them out: surely he shall make their habitations desolate with them. <hi type="super">21</hi> The earth is moved at the noise of their fall, at the cry the noise thereof was heard in the Red sea. <hi type="super">22</hi> Behold, he shall come up and fly as the eagle, and spread his wings over Bozrah: and at that day shall the heart of the mighty men of Edom be as the heart of a woman in her pangs. <div eID="gen18168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18169" type="x-p"/> The Edomites come next to receive their doom from God, by the mouth of Jeremiah: they also were old enemies to the Israel of God; but their day will come to be reckoned with, and it is now at hand, and is foretold, not only for warning to them, but for comfort to the Israel of God, whose afflictions were very much aggravated by their triumphs over them and joy in their calamity, <reference osisRef="Ps.137.7">Ps. cxxxvii. 7</reference>. Many of the expressions used in this prophecy <hi type="italic">concerning Edom</hi> are borrowed from the prophecy of Obadiah, which is <hi type="italic">concerning Edom;</hi> for, all the prophets being inspired by one and the same Spirit, there must needs be a wonderful harmony and agreement in their predictions. Now here it is foretold, <div eID="gen18169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18170" type="x-p"/> I. That the country of Edom should be all wasted and made desolate, that <hi type="italic">the calamity of Esau</hi> should be <hi type="italic">brought upon him,</hi> the calamity he has deserved, and God has long designed him, for his old sins, <reference osisRef="Jer.49.8">v. 8</reference>. The time is at hand when God <hi type="italic">will visit him,</hi> and call him to an account, and then they shall <hi type="italic">flee</hi> from the sword, <hi type="italic">turn back</hi> from the battle, and <hi type="italic">dwell deep</hi> in some close caverns, where they shall hide themselves. All they have shall be carried off by the conqueror; whereas <hi type="italic">grape-gatherers</hi> will <hi type="italic">leave some gleanings,</hi> and even <hi type="italic">thieves</hi> know when <hi type="italic">they have enough</hi> and <hi type="italic">will destroy</hi> no further, those that destroy them shall never be satiated, (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.9-Jer.49.10">v. 9, 10</reference>); they shall make <hi type="italic">Esau</hi> quite <hi type="italic">bare,</hi> shall strip the Edomites of all they have, shall find out ways and means to come at their most hidden treasure, shall discover even the <hi type="italic">secret places</hi> where they thought to secure their wealth, and rifle them, so that they shall none of them save their wealth, no, nor save themselves nor their children, that might be concealed in a little room: <hi type="italic">He shall not be able to hide himself,</hi> and <hi type="italic">his seed</hi> too <hi type="italic">is spoiled. His brethren</hi> the Moabites, <hi type="italic">and his neighbours</hi> the Philistines, whom he might have expected succours from, or at least shelter with, are spoiled as well as he and disabled to do him any service. <hi type="italic">And he is not,</hi> or <hi type="italic">there is not he, there is none to him, none left him,</hi> that may say what follows (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.11">v. 11</reference>), <hi type="italic">Leave thy fatherless children, I will preserve them alive.</hi> When they are flying, or dying, there shall be none left, no relation, no friend, no, not so much as any parish officers to take care of their wives and children that they leave behind. Edom is not, he is cut off and gone; nor is there any to say, <hi type="italic">Leave me thy orphans.</hi> If the master of a family be cut off, or forced away, it is some comfort if he have a friend to leave his family with, whom he can confide in; but they shall have none such, for they shall all be involved in the same calamity. The Chaldee makes these to be the words of God to his people, distinguishing them from the Edomites in this calamity; and they read it, "<hi type="italic">But you, O house of Israel! you shall not leave your orphans; I will secure them, and let your widows rest on my word.</hi> Whatever becomes of the widows and fatherless of the Edomites, I will take care of yours." Note, it is an unspeakable comfort to the people of God, when they are dying, that they may leave their surviving relations with God, may, in faith, commit them to him and encourage them to trust in him; and, though they cannot promise themselves great things in the world for them, yet they may hope that he will preserve them alive, always, provided that they trust in him. Let the Edomites, for their part, count upon no other than to be made <hi type="italic">a desolation</hi> and <hi type="italic">a reproach;</hi> for the decree has gone forth; God hath <hi type="italic">sworn it by himself</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.13">v. 13</reference>), that their <hi type="italic">cities shall be wasted,</hi> nay, they <hi type="italic">shall be perpetual wastes,</hi> they shall be made mean and despicable; they had made a mighty figure, but God will make <hi type="italic">them small among the heathen;</hi> and those that despised God's people shall themselves be <hi type="italic">despised among men</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.15">v. 15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Obad.1.2">Obad. 2</reference>), nay, they shall be made monstrous, and even a prodigy (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">Edom shall be</hi> such a <hi type="italic">desolation</hi> that every one who goes by <hi type="italic">shall be astonished;</hi> nay, worse yet, they shall be made a terror; Edom shall be made like Sodom and Gomorrah, none shall care for coming near the ruins of it, <hi type="italic">no man shall abide there</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.18">v. 18</reference>), such a frightful place shall it be made. <div eID="gen18170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18171" type="x-p"/> II. That the instruments of this destruction should be very resolute and formidable. They have their commission from God; he summons them into this service (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">I have heard a rumour,</hi> or report, <hi type="italic">from the Lord,</hi> heard it by the prophecy of Obadiah, heard it by a whisper to myself, that <hi type="italic">an ambassador,</hi> or herald, or messenger, <hi type="italic">is sent to the</hi> Gentiles, who are to lay Edom waste, <hi type="italic">saying, Gather you together,</hi> muster all the forces you can, <hi type="italic">and come against her;</hi> for (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.20">v. 20</reference>) this is <hi type="italic">the counsel that he hath taken against Edom.</hi> The matter is settled, the decree has gone forth, and there is no resisting it. God has determined that Edom shall be laid waste, and then he that is to be employed in wasting it shall come swiftly and strongly. Nebuchadnezzar is he or whom it is here foretold, 1. That he <hi type="italic">shall come up like a lion,</hi> with fierceness and fury, like a lion enraged by <hi type="italic">the swelling of Jordan</hi> overflowing his banks, which forces him out of his covert by the water-side into the higher grounds, <reference osisRef="Jer.49.19">v. 19</reference>. He shall come roaring, come to devour all that come in his way. He shall <hi type="italic">come against the habitation of the strong,</hi> the forts and castles; and I <hi type="italic">will cause him to come suddenly into the land</hi> (so the next words might well be read), so as to find them unprovided with necessaries for a defence; for I will look out <hi type="italic">a chosen man to appoint over her,</hi> to do this execution, a man fit for the purpose, one chosen out of the people; for when God has work to do he will find out the fittest instruments to be employed in doing it: "<hi type="italic">Who is like me</hi> for choosing the instruments, and spiriting them for the work? And <hi type="italic">who will appoint me the time?</hi> Who will challenge me, and fix a time and place to meet me? Who will join issue with me in battle? And, when I send a lion into the flock, <hi type="italic">who is that shepherd</hi> that can, or dare, stand before me, or against me, to oppose that lion, and think to rescue any of the flock?" Note, When God has work to do of any kind he will soon find those that are able to engage in it, and all the world cannot find those that are able to engage against it. Nay, if God will have Edom destroyed, and their peopled dislodged, there needs not a lion, a fierce lion to do it: <hi type="italic">Even the least of the flock shall draw them out</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.20">v. 20</reference>); the meanest servant in Nebuchadnezzar's retinue, the weakest of all that follow his camp, shall <hi type="italic">draw them out</hi> for the slaughter, shall force them to flee, or to surrender, and <hi type="italic">make their habitations desolate with them.</hi> God can bring to pass the greatest works by instruments least likely. When the Chaldean army comes against the Edomites all hands shall be employed and the poorest soldier in it shall have a pluck at them. 2. Nebuchadnezzar shall come, not only like a lion, the king of beasts, but like an eagle, the king of birds (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.22">v. 22</reference>): <hi type="italic">He shall fly as the eagle</hi> upon his prey, so swiftly, so strongly, shall clap his wings upon Bozrah, to secure it for himself (as before, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.40">ch. xlviii. 40</reference>), and immediately <hi type="italic">the hearts of the mighty men</hi> shall fail them, for they shall see he is an enemy that it is in vain to struggle with. <div eID="gen18171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18172" type="x-p"/> III. That the Edomites' confidences should all fail them in the day of their distress. 1. They trusted to their wisdom, but that shall stand them in no stead. This is the first thing fastened upon in this prophecy against Edom, <reference osisRef="Jer.49.7">v. 7</reference>. That nation used to be famous for wisdom, and their statesmen were thought to excel in politics; and yet now they shall take such wrong measures in all their counsels, and be so baffled in all their designs, that people shall ask, with wonder, What is the matter with the Edomites? <hi type="italic">Is wisdom no more in Teman?</hi> Have the wise men of the east country (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.30">1 Kings iv. 30</reference>) become fools? Are those at <hi type="italic">their wits' end</hi> that were thought to have the monopoly of prudence? <hi type="italic">Has counsel perished from the understanding men?</hi> It is so, when God is designing the ruin of a people; for whom he will destroy he infatuates. See <reference osisRef="Job.12.20">Job xii. 20</reference>. <hi type="italic">Has their wisdom vanished? Is it tired?</hi> (so some); <hi type="italic">is it worn out?</hi> (so others); <hi type="italic">has it become useless?</hi> so others. Yes, it will do them no service when God comes forth to contend with them. 2. They trusted to their strength, but neither shall that avail them, <reference osisRef="Jer.49.16">v. 16</reference>. They had been a terror to all their neighbours; every body feared them and truckled to them, and this made them proud and conceited of themselves and their own strength, and very secure; because no neighbouring nation durst meddle with them, they thought no nation in the world durst. Their country was much of it mountainous, having many passes which they thought themselves able to make good against any invader; but this terribleness of theirs deceived them, and so did their imaginary inaccessibleness; they did not prove so strong as they were formidable, nor so safe as they were secure. High as they are, God will bring them down; for, as <hi type="italic">there is no wisdom,</hi> so there is no might <hi type="italic">against the Lord,</hi> See these expressions, <reference osisRef="Obad.1.3-Obad.1.4">Obad. 3, 4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Obad.1.8">8</reference>. <div eID="gen18172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18173" type="x-p"/> IV. That their destruction should be inevitable and very remarkable. 1. God hath determined it (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.12">v. 12</reference>); he hath said it; nay (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.13">v. 13</reference>), he hath <hi type="italic">sworn it,</hi> that <hi type="italic">the Edomites shall not go unpunished,</hi> but that they shall <hi type="italic">drink the cup of trembling,</hi> which is put into the hands of all their neighbours; even those <hi type="italic">whose judgment,</hi> or doom, <hi type="italic">was not to drink of the cup,</hi> who had not so well deserved it as they had done, nations that had not been such enemies to Israel as they had been, or Israel itself, that was God's peculiar people, and among whom there were many, very many, who kept his ordinances, upon which account they might have expected an exemption; and yet they had been made to drink of the bitter cup; and shall the Edomites think to pass it? No; they shall <hi type="italic">surely drink of it.</hi> Note, When God punishes the less guilty it is folly for the more guilty to promise themselves impunity; and when judgment begins at God's house it will reach the strangers. 2. All the world shall take notice of it (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.21">v. 21</reference>): <hi type="italic">The earth is moved,</hi> and all the nations are put into a concern, <hi type="italic">at the noise of their fall;</hi> the news of it shall make them tremble. <hi type="italic">The noise of the outcry is heard to the Red Sea,</hi> which flowed upon the coasts of Edom. So loud shall be the shouts of the conquerors and the shrieks of the conquered, and such a mighty noise shall the news of this destruction of Idumea make in the nations, that is shall be heard among the ships that lie in the Red Sea to take in lading (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.9.26">1 Kings ix. 26</reference>), and then they shall carry the news of it to the remotest shore. Note, The fall of those who have affected to make a noise with their pomp and power will make so much the greater noise.
entries.107be41e66a2d8269aad7ae6bf6e257839c7192b: <div eID="gen18173" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Judgment of Damascus. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 595.)</title> <div sID="gen18174" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> Concerning Damascus. Hamath is confounded, and Arpad: for they have heard evil tidings: they are faint hearted; <hi type="italic">there is</hi> sorrow on the sea; it cannot be quiet. <hi type="super">24</hi> Damascus is waxed feeble, <hi type="italic">and</hi> turneth herself to flee, and fear hath seized on <hi type="italic">her:</hi> anguish and sorrows have taken her, as a woman in travail. <hi type="super">25</hi> How is the city of praise not left, the city of my joy! <hi type="super">26</hi> Therefore her young men shall fall in her streets, and all the men of war shall be cut off in that day, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts. <hi type="super">27</hi> And I will kindle a fire in the wall of Damascus, and it shall consume the palaces of Benhadad. <div eID="gen18174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18175" type="x-p"/> The kingdom of Syria lay north of Canaan, as that of Edom lay south, and thither we must now remove and take a view of the approaching fate of that kingdom, which had been often vexatious to the Israel of God. Damascus was the metropolis of that kingdom, and the ruin of the whole is supposed in the ruin of that: yet Hamath and Arpad, two other considerable cities, are names (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.23">v. 23</reference>), and <hi type="italic">the palaces of Ben-hadad,</hi> which he built, are particularly marked for ruin, <reference osisRef="Jer.49.27">v. 27</reference>; see also <reference osisRef="Amos.1.4">Amos i. 4</reference>. Some think Ben-hadad (the son of Hadad, either their idol, or one of their ancient kings, whence the rest descended) was a common name of the kings of Syria, as Pharaoh of the kings of Egypt. Now observe concerning the judgment of Damascus, 1. It begins with a terrible fright and faint-heartedness. They <hi type="italic">hear evil tidings,</hi> that the king of Babylon, with all his force, is coming against them, and <hi type="italic">they are confounded;</hi> they know not what measures to take for their own safety, their souls are melted, <hi type="italic">they are faint-hearted,</hi> they have no spirit left them, they are like <hi type="italic">the troubled sea, that cannot be quiet</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.57.20">Isa. lvii. 20</reference>), or like men <hi type="italic">in a storm</hi> at sea (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.26">Ps. xvii. 26</reference>); or the sorrow that begins in the city shall go to the sea-coast, <reference osisRef="Jer.49.23">v. 23</reference>. See how easily God can dispirit those nations that have been most celebrated for valour. <hi type="italic">Damascus</hi> now <hi type="italic">waxes feeble</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.24">v. 24</reference>), a city that thought she could look the most formidable enemy in the face now <hi type="italic">turns herself to flee,</hi> and owns it is to no more purpose to think of contending with her fate than for <hi type="italic">a woman in</hi> labour to contend with her pains, which she cannot escape, but must yield to. It was a <hi type="italic">city of praise</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.25">v. 25</reference>), not praise to God, but to herself, a city much commended and admired by all strangers that visited it. It was a <hi type="italic">city of joy,</hi> where there was an affluence and confluence of all the delights of the sons of men, and abundance of mirth in the enjoyment of them. We read it (though there is no necessity for this) <hi type="italic">the city of my joy,</hi> which the prophet himself had sometimes visited with pleasure. Or it may be the speech of the king lamenting the ruin of <hi type="italic">the city of</hi> his <hi type="italic">joy.</hi> But now it is all overwhelmed with fear and grief. Note, Those deceive themselves who place their happiness in carnal joys; for God in his providence can soon cast a damp upon them and put an end to them. He can soon make a <hi type="italic">city of praise</hi> to be a reproach and a <hi type="italic">city of joy</hi> to be a terror to itself. 2. It ends with a terrible fall and fire. (1.) The inhabitants are slain (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.26">v. 26</reference>): The <hi type="italic">young men,</hi> who should fight the enemy and defend the city, <hi type="italic">shall fall</hi> by the sword <hi type="italic">in her streets; and all the men of war,</hi> mighty men, expert in war, and engaged in the service of their country, <hi type="italic">shall be cut off.</hi> (2.) The city is laid in ashes (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.27">v. 27</reference>): The <hi type="italic">fire</hi> is <hi type="italic">kindled</hi> by the besiegers <hi type="italic">in the wall,</hi> but it shall devour all before it, <hi type="italic">the palaces of Ben-hadad</hi> particularly, where so much mischief had formerly been hatched against God's Israel, for which it is now thus visited.
entries.2d2921e8ed709d271f512ed3900bf86c98c21d35: <div eID="gen18175" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Judgment of Kedar. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 595.)</title> <div sID="gen18176" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">28</hi> Concerning Kedar, and concerning the kingdoms of Hazor, which Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon shall smite, thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; Arise ye, go up to Kedar, and spoil the men of the east. <hi type="super">29</hi> Their tents and their flocks shall they take away: they shall take to themselves their curtains, and all their vessels, and their camels; and they shall cry unto them, Fear <hi type="italic">is</hi> on every side. <hi type="super">30</hi> Flee, get you far off, dwell deep, O ye inhabitants of Hazor, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; for Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon hath taken counsel against you, and hath conceived a purpose against you. <hi type="super">31</hi> Arise, get you up unto the wealthy nation, that dwelleth without care, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , which have neither gates nor bars, <hi type="italic">which</hi> dwell alone. <hi type="super">32</hi> And their camels shall be a booty, and the multitude of their cattle a spoil: and I will scatter into all winds them <hi type="italic">that are</hi> in the utmost corners; and I will bring their calamity from all sides thereof, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">33</hi> And Hazor shall be a dwelling for dragons, <hi type="italic">and</hi> a desolation for ever: there shall no man abide there, nor <hi type="italic">any</hi> son of man dwell in it. <div eID="gen18176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18177" type="x-p"/> These verses foretell the desolation that Nebuchadnezzar and his forces should make among the people of Kedar (who descended from Kedar the son of Ishmael, and inhabited a part of Arabia the Stony), and of the kingdoms, the petty principalities, of Hazor, that joined to them, who perhaps were originally Canaanites, of the kingdom of Hazor, in the north of Canaan, which had Jabin for its king, but, being driven thence, settled in the deserts of Arabia and associated themselves with the Kedarenes. Concerning this people we may here observe, <div eID="gen18177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18178" type="x-p"/> I. What was their present state and posture? They dwelt in <hi type="italic">tents</hi> and had no walls, but <hi type="italic">curtains</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.20">v. 20</reference>), no fortified cities; they had <hi type="italic">neither gates nor bars,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.49.31">v. 31</reference>. They were shepherds, and had no treasures, but stock upon land, no money, but flocks and camels. They had no soldiers among them, for they were in no fear of invaders, no merchants, for they <hi type="italic">dwelt alone,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.49.31">v. 31</reference>. Those of other nations neither came among them nor traded with them; but they lived within themselves, content with the products and pleasures of their own country. This was their manner of living, very different from that of the nations that were round about them. And, 1. They were very rich; though they had not trade, no treasures, yet they are here said to be a <hi type="italic">wealthy nation</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.31">v. 31</reference>), because they had a sufficiency to answer all the occasions of human life and they were content with it. Note, Those are truly rich who have enough to supply their necessities, and know when they have enough. We need not go to the treasures of kings and provinces, or to the cash of merchants, to look for wealthy people; they may be found among shepherds <hi type="italic">that dwell in tents.</hi> 2. They were very easy: <hi type="italic">They dwelt without care.</hi> Their wealth was such as nobody envied them, or, if any did, they might come peaceably and enjoy the like; and therefore they feared nobody. Note, Those that live innocently and honestly may live very securely, though they have <hi type="italic">neither gates nor bars.</hi> <div eID="gen18178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18179" type="x-p"/> II. The design of the king of Babylon against them and the descent he make upon them: <hi type="italic">He has taken counsel against you and has conceived a purpose against you,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.49.30">v. 30</reference>. That proud man resolves it shall never be said that he, who had conquered so many strong cities, will leave those unconquered <hi type="italic">that dwell in tents.</hi> It was strange that that eagle should stoop to catch these flies, that so great a prince should play at such small game; but all is fish that comes to the ambitious covetous man's net. Note, It will not always secure men from suffering wrong to be able to say that they have done no wrong; not to have given offence will not be a defence against such men as Nebuchadnezzar. Yet, how unrighteous soever he was in doing it, God was righteous in directing it. These people had lived inoffensively among their neighbours, as many do, who yet, like them, are guilty before God; and it was to punish them for their offences against him that God said (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.28">v. 28</reference>): <hi type="italic">Arise, go up to Kedar, and spoil the men of the east.</hi> They will do it to gratify their own covetousness and ambition, but God orders it for the correcting of an unthankful people, and for warning to a careless world to expect trouble when they seem to be most safe. God says to the Chaldeans (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.31">v. 31</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Arise, get up to the wealthy nation that dwells without care;</hi> go and give them an alarm, that none may imagine <hi type="italic">their mountain stands so strong that it cannot be moved.</hi>" <div eID="gen18179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18180" type="x-p"/> III. The great amazement that this put them into, and the great desolation hereby made among them: <hi type="italic">They shall cry unto them;</hi> those on the borders shall send the alarm into all parts of the country, which shall be put into the utmost confusion by it; they shall cry, "<hi type="italic">Fear is on every side</hi>—We are surrounded by the enemy." the very terror of which shall drive them all to their feet and they shall none of them have any heart to make resistance. The enemy shall <hi type="italic">proclaim fear upon them,</hi> or <hi type="italic">against them, on every side.</hi> They need not strike a stroke; they shall shout them out of their tents, <reference osisRef="Jer.49.29">v. 29</reference>. Upon the first alarm, they shall <hi type="italic">flee, get far off,</hi> and <hi type="italic">dwell deep</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.30">v. 30</reference>), as the Edomites, <reference osisRef="Jer.49.8">v. 8</reference>. And it will be found that this <hi type="italic">fear on every side</hi> is not groundless, for <hi type="italic">their calamity</hi> shall be <hi type="italic">brought from all sides thereof,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.49.31">v. 31</reference>. No marvel there are <hi type="italic">fears on every side</hi> when there are foes on every side. The issue will be, 1. What they have will be a prey to the Chaldeans; they shall <hi type="italic">take to themselves their curtains and vessels;</hi> though they are but plain and coarse, and they have better of their own, yet they shall take them for spite, and spoil for spoiling sake. <hi type="italic">They shall carry away their tents and their flocks,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.49.29">v. 29</reference>. <hi type="italic">Their camels</hi> shall be a booty to those that came for nothing else, <reference osisRef="Jer.49.31">v. 31</reference>. 2. It is not said that any of them shall be slain, for they attempt not to make any resistance and their tents and flocks are accepted as a ransom for their lives; but they shall be dislodged and dispersed; though now they dwell <hi type="italic">in the utmost corners,</hi> out of the way, and therefore they think out of the reach, of danger (by this character those people were distinguished, <reference osisRef="Jer.9.23">ch. ix. 26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.9.25">25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.9.26">23</reference>), yet they shall be <hi type="italic">scattered</hi> thence <hi type="italic">into all winds,</hi> into all parts of the world. Note, Privacy and obscurity are not always a protection and security. Many that affect to be strangers to the world may yet by unthought-of providences be forced into it; and those that live most retired may have the same lot with those that thrust themselves forth and lie most exposed. 3. Their country shall lie uninhabited; for, lying remote and out of all high roads, and having neither cities nor lands inviting to strangers, none shall care to succeed them, so that <hi type="italic">Hazor shall be a desolation for ever,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.49.33">v. 33</reference>. If busy men be displaced, many strive to get into their placed, because they lived great; but here are easy quiet men displaced, and <hi type="italic">no man</hi> cared to <hi type="italic">abide</hi> where they did, because they lived meanly.
entries.770cc5cdd9eee7578c6337048925cbe825cc9c1f: <div eID="gen18180" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Judgment of Elam. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 595.)</title> <div sID="gen18181" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">34</hi> The word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> that came to Jeremiah the prophet against Elam in the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah king of Judah, saying, <hi type="super">35</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts; Behold, I will break the bow of Elam, the chief of their might. <hi type="super">36</hi> And upon Elam will I bring the four winds from the four quarters of heaven, and will scatter them toward all those winds; and there shall be no nation whither the outcasts of Elam shall not come. <hi type="super">37</hi> For I will cause Elam to be dismayed before their enemies, and before them that seek their life: and I will bring evil upon them, <hi type="italic">even</hi> my fierce anger, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; and I will send the sword after them, till I have consumed them: <hi type="super">38</hi> And I will set my throne in Elam, and will destroy from thence the king and the princes, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">39</hi> But it shall come to pass in the latter days, <hi type="italic">that</hi> I will bring again the captivity of Elam, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen18181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18182" type="x-p"/> This prophecy is dated in the beginning of Zedekiah's reign; it is probable that the other prophecies against the Gentiles, going before, were at the same time. The Elamites were the Persians, descended from Elam the son of Shem (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.22">Gen. x. 22</reference>); yet some think it was only that part of Persia which lay nearest to the Jews which was called <hi type="italic">Elymais,</hi> and adjoined to Media-Elam, which, say they, had acted against God's Israel, <hi type="italic">bore the quiver</hi> in an expedition against them (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.6">Isa. xxii. 6</reference>), and therefore must be reckoned with among the rest. It is here foretold, in general, that God will <hi type="italic">bring evil upon them, even</hi> his <hi type="italic">fierce anger,</hi> and that is evil enough, it has <hi type="italic">all evil in it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.49.37">v. 37</reference>. In particular, 1. Their forces shall be disabled, and rendered incapable of doing them any service. The Elamites were famous archers, but, <hi type="italic">Behold, I will break the bow of Elam</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.35">v. 35</reference>), will ruin their artillery, and then <hi type="italic">the chief of their might</hi> is gone. God often orders it so that that which we most trust to first fails us, and that which was <hi type="italic">the chief of our might</hi> proves the least of our help. 2. Their people shall be dispersed. There shall come enemies against them from all parts of the world, and they shall all carry some of them away captive into their respective countries; while others shall flee, some one way and some another, to shift for themselves, so that <hi type="italic">there shall be no nation whither the outcasts of Elam shall not come,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.49.36">v. 36</reference>. <hi type="italic">The four winds</hi> shall be brought upon them; the storm shall come sometimes from one point and sometimes from another, to toss and hurry them several ways. We know not from what point the wind of trouble may blow; but, if God encompass us with his favour, we are safe, and may be easy, which way soever the storm comes. Fear shall drive them into other countries; they shall <hi type="italic">be dismayed before their enemies;</hi> but, as if that were not enough, <hi type="italic">I will send the sword after them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.49.37">v. 37</reference>. Note, God can make his judgments follow those that think by flight to escape them and to get out of the reach of them. <hi type="italic">Evil pursues sinners.</hi> 3. Their princes shall be destroyed and the government quite changed (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.38">v. 38</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will set my throne in Elam.</hi> The throne of Nebuchadnezzar shall be set there, or the throne of Cyrus, who began his conquests with Elymais. Or it may be meant of the throne on which God sits for judgment; he will make them know that he reigns, that he <hi type="italic">judges in the earth,</hi> that <hi type="italic">kings and princes</hi> are accountable to him, and that high as they are he is above them. The king of Elam was famous of old, <reference osisRef="Gen.14.1">Gen. xiv. 1</reference>. Chedorlaomer was king of Elam, and a mighty man he was in his day; the nations about him served him; his successors, we may suppose, made a great figure; but the king of Elam is no more to God than another man. When God <hi type="italic">sets his throne in Elam</hi> he <hi type="italic">will destroy thence the king and the princes</hi> that are, and set up whom he pleases. 4. Yet the destruction of Elam shall not be perpetual (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.39">v. 39</reference>): <hi type="italic">In the latter days I will bring again the captivity of Elam.</hi> When Cyrus had destroyed Babylon, brought the empire into the hands of the Persians, the Elamites no doubt returned in triumph out of all the countries whither they were scattered, and settled again in their own country. But this promise was to have its full and principal accomplishment in the days of the Messiah, when we find Elamites particularly among those who, when the Holy Ghost was given, heard spoken <hi type="italic">in their own tongues the wonderful works of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.9">Acts ii. 9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.2.11">11</reference>), and that is the most desirable return of the captivity. <hi type="italic">If the Son make you free, then you shall be free indeed.</hi>  <chapter eID="Jer.49"/> <div eID="gen18182" type="x-p"/>

entries.afba948699822ddafecc84fe18f98c062d33d37e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10630"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 49</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Jer.49.1-Jer.49.39">Jr 49:1-39</reference>. Predictions as to Ammon, Idumea, Damascus, Kedar, Hazor, and Elam.</title> <div sID="gen18998" type="x-p"/> The event of the prophecy as to Ammon preceded that as to Moab (see on <reference osisRef="Jer.49.3">Jr 49:3</reference>); and in <reference osisRef="Ezek.21.26-Ezek.21.28">Eze 21:26-28</reference>, the destruction of Ammon is subjoined to the deposition of Zedekiah.<div eID="gen18998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18999" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10630"/><hi type="bold">1. Hath Israel ... no heir?--</hi>namely, to occupy the land of Gad, after it itself has been carried away captive by Shalmaneser. Ammon, like Moab, descended from Lot, lay north of Moab, from which it was separated by the river Arnon, and east of Reuben and Gad (<reference osisRef="Josh.13.24">Jos 13:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.13.25">25</reference>) on the same side of Jordan. It seized on Gad when Israel was carried captive. Judah was by the right of kindred the heir, not Ammon; but Ammon joined with Nebuchadnezzar against Judah and Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.2">2Ki 24:2</reference>) and exulted over its fall (<reference osisRef="Ps.83.4-Ps.7.8">Psa 83:4-7, 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zeph.2.8">Zep 2:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.9">9</reference>). It had already, in the days of Jeroboam, in Israel's affliction, tried to "enlarge its border" (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.26">2Ki 14:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.1.1">Am 1:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.13">13</reference>).<div eID="gen18999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19000" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">their king--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Amos.1.15">Am 1:15</reference>); referring to Melchom, their tutelary idol (<reference osisRef="Zeph.1.5">Zep 1:5</reference>); and so the Septuagint reads it here as a proper name (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.5">1Ki 11:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.33">33</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.13">2Ki 23:13</reference>). The Ammonite god is said to do what they do, namely, occupy the Israelite land of Gad. To Jehovah, the theocratic "King" of Israel, the land belonged of right; so that their Molech or Melchom was a usurper-king.<div eID="gen19000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19001" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his people--</hi>the people of Melchom, "their king." Compare "people of Chemosh," <reference osisRef="Jer.48.46">Jr 48:46</reference>. <div eID="gen19001" type="x-p"/>
entries.4f5d548a3fbcdc414a5056e0f6b57b6dc6ebce23: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10631"/><div sID="gen19002" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10631"/><hi type="bold">2. Rabbah--</hi>"the great," metropolis of Ammon (<reference osisRef="2Sam.12.26-2Sam.12.30">2Sa 12:26-30</reference>). Its destruction is foretold also in <reference osisRef="Ezek.25.5">Eze 25:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.1.14">Am 1:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.15">15</reference>.<div eID="gen19002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19003" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">her daughters--</hi>the towns and villages, dependencies of the metropolis (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.45">Jos 15:45</reference>).<div eID="gen19003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19004" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall ... be heir--</hi>shall possess those who possessed him. The full accomplishment of this is still future; partially fulfilled under the Maccabees (1 Maccabees 5:6). <div eID="gen19004" type="x-p"/>
entries.5147337eac29da9994f1d2431b86216c3f8e93c9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10632"/><div sID="gen19005" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10632"/><hi type="bold">3. Heshbon ... Ai--</hi>Nebuchadnezzar, coming from the north, first attacked Ammon, then its brother and neighbor, Moab. As Ai of Ammon had already suffered destruction, Heshbon of Moab being near it might well fear the same fate.<div eID="gen19005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19006" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hedges--</hi>Their cities being destroyed, the outcasts have no place of shelter save behind the "hedges" of vineyards and gardens; or else the enclosures of their villages.<div eID="gen19006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19007" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">their king--</hi>Melchom, the idol, as the mention of "his priests" shows (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.48.7">Jr 48:7</reference>). <div eID="gen19007" type="x-p"/>
entries.48ecf570dde9f5f01bac6ff91ecc84c0c733abc2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10633"/><div sID="gen19008" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10633"/><hi type="bold">4. thy flowing valley--</hi>rather, "thy valley shall flow," namely with the blood of the slain; in sad contrast to their "valleys" in which they had heretofore "gloried," as flowing with milk and honey [Grotius]. Or else, as Margin, "shall flow away."<div eID="gen19008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19009" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">backsliding--</hi>apostate from Jehovah, the God of their father Lot, to Molech.<div eID="gen19009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19010" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">treasures--</hi>her resources for resisting the foe.<div eID="gen19010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19011" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Who shall, &c.--</hi>Who can come ... (<reference osisRef="Jer.21.13">Jr 21:13</reference>). <div eID="gen19011" type="x-p"/>
entries.0ea10193cd1a402afe290c61ae28dd765eff7c9a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10634"/><div sID="gen19012" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10634"/><hi type="bold">5. every man right forth--</hi>whithersoever chance may lead him (<reference osisRef="Jer.46.5">Jr 46:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.19.17">Ge 19:17</reference>); straight before him, onwards at random (<reference osisRef="Amos.4.3">Am 4:3</reference>).<div eID="gen19012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19013" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">none ... gather up him, &c.--</hi>There shall be none to gather together the wandering fugitives, so as to care for them and restore them to their own homes. <div eID="gen19013" type="x-p"/>
entries.c37bd9dbc761ad6ade6dcc90a8fdfb5250ebabd9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10635"/><div sID="gen19014" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10635"/>6. (Compare <reference osisRef="Jer.48.47">Jr 48:47</reference>). For the sake of "righteous" Lot their progenitor. Partially fulfilled under Cyrus; in gospel times more fully. <div eID="gen19014" type="x-p"/>
entries.3da09cc0163d84002e931dad38c46b7108a88684: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10636"/><div sID="gen19015" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10636"/><hi type="bold">7. Concerning Edom--</hi>a distinct prophecy, copied in part from Obadiah, but with the freedom of one himself inspired and foretelling a later calamity. Obadiah's was fulfilled probably in Sennacherib's time (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.34.5">Is 34:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.1.11">Am 1:11</reference>); Jeremiah's about the same time as his preceding prophecies (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.12">Jr 49:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.25.12">Eze 25:12</reference>).<div eID="gen19015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19016" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wisdom--</hi>for which the Arabs and the people of Teman (a city of Edom) in particular, were famed (<reference osisRef="Gen.36.15">Ge 36:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.30">1Ki 4:30</reference>; see Job, everywhere; Ob 8).<div eID="gen19016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19017" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">vanished--</hi>literally, "poured out," that is, exhausted (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.19.3">Is 19:3</reference>, Margin) [Maurer]. Or, as the kindred Ethiopic word means, "worn out" [Ludovicus De Dieu]. <div eID="gen19017" type="x-p"/>
entries.235081883c53d7fd50280a63eaf2284566571768: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10637"/><div sID="gen19018" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10637"/><hi type="bold">8. turn--</hi>namely, your backs in flight.<div eID="gen19018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19019" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dwell deep--</hi>in deep defiles and caves [Grotius], which abound in Idumea. Others refer it to the Arab custom of retiring into the depth of the desert when avoiding an offended foe (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.30">Jr 49:30</reference>).<div eID="gen19019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19020" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Dedan--</hi>a tribe bordering on and made subject by Idumea; descended from Jokshan, son of Abraham and Keturah (<reference osisRef="Gen.25.1-Gen.25.3">Ge 25:1-3</reference>).<div eID="gen19020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19021" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Esau--</hi>The naming of Edom's progenitor, reprobated by God, recalls the remembrance of the old curse on him for his profanity, both his sin and its punishment being perpetuated in his descendants (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.16">He 12:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.17">17</reference>). <div eID="gen19021" type="x-p"/>
entries.ea49e4b386ad63c5e5859eb8b76dde421d53768a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10638"/><div sID="gen19022" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10638"/>9. (Ob 5). Grape gatherers, yea even thieves, leave something behind them; but the Chaldeans will sweep Idumea clean of everything. <div eID="gen19022" type="x-p"/>
entries.be4f1747742f3bfb62e2a91ae13acd2e48491856: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10639"/><div sID="gen19023" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10639"/>10. Edom became politically extinct after the time of the Romans.<div eID="gen19023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19024" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">uncovered his secret places--</hi>where he hid himself (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.8">Jr 49:8</reference>) and his treasures (<reference osisRef="Isa.45.3">Is 45:3</reference>). I have caused that nothing should be so hidden as that the conqueror should not find it.<div eID="gen19024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19025" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">brethren--</hi>Ammon.<div eID="gen19025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19026" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neighbours--</hi>the Philistines. <div eID="gen19026" type="x-p"/>
entries.80059bce1e06f8649993f095f6c738ec55705339: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10640"/><div sID="gen19027" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10640"/>11. Thy fatherless and widows must rest their hope in God alone, as none of the adult males shall be left alive, so desperate will be the affairs of Edom. The verse also, besides this threat, implies a promise of mercy to Esau in God's good time, as there was to Moab and Ammon (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.6">Jr 49:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.48.47">Jr 48:47</reference>); the extinction of the adult males is the prominent idea (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.49.12">Jr 49:12</reference>). <div eID="gen19027" type="x-p"/>
entries.f341c32ebcc4cd411a56f9ade508f064963136d1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10641"/><div sID="gen19028" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10641"/>12. (Compare <reference osisRef="Jer.25.15">Jr 25:15</reference>, 16, 29).<div eID="gen19028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19029" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they whose judgment was not to drink of the cup--</hi>the Jews to whom, by virtue of the covenant relation, it did not belong to drink the cup. It might have been expected that they would be spared. He regards not the merits of the Jews, for they were as bad or worse than others: but the grace and adoption of God; it is just and natural ("judgment") that God should pardon His sons sooner than aliens [Calvin]. <div eID="gen19029" type="x-p"/>
entries.15760e5e68e990707f7fb053af117c05391085b7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10642"/><div sID="gen19030" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10642"/><hi type="bold">13. Bozrah--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Jer.48.24">Jr 48:24</reference>). <div eID="gen19030" type="x-p"/>
entries.7f53ab520985972c12a87ba77aa25377bc266cbe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10643"/><div sID="gen19031" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10643"/>14. (Ob 1-3).<div eID="gen19031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19032" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ambassador ... unto the heathen--</hi>a messenger from God to stir up the Chaldeans against Edom. <div eID="gen19032" type="x-p"/>
entries.c5df38c48d35796ea8a0827195b60c98df526923: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10644"/><div sID="gen19033" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10644"/>15. David and Joab had already humbled Edom (<reference osisRef="2Sam.8.14">2Sa 8:14</reference>). <div eID="gen19033" type="x-p"/>
entries.b8e856886f00ef0a7a6624dfb39e54f44452200b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10645"/><div sID="gen19034" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10645"/><hi type="bold">16. terribleness--</hi>the terror which thou didst inspire into others.<div eID="gen19034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19035" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">deceived thee--</hi>rendered thee proudly confident, as if none would dare to assail thee.<div eID="gen19035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19036" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dwellest in ... rock--</hi>Petra, the chief of Idumea, was cut in the rocks; its ruins are very remarkable. The whole south of Idumea abounds in cave dwellings and rocks.<div eID="gen19036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19037" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">though ... nest ... eagle--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Job.39.27">Job 39:27</reference>; Ob 3, 4). The eagle builds its nest in the highest craggy eyry. <div eID="gen19037" type="x-p"/>
entries.3fd7ca741e1a35262aadac138b9b1ca2f540817e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10646"/><div sID="gen19038" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10646"/>17. (Compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.9.8">1Ki 9:8</reference>). <div eID="gen19038" type="x-p"/>
entries.eb9b732742748cd0d2e72aa838474ac3952ffcda: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10647"/><div sID="gen19039" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10647"/>18. (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.40">Jr 50:40</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.29.23">De 29:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.4.11">Am 4:11</reference>).<div eID="gen19039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19040" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no man shall abide there--</hi>that is, of the Idumeans. The Romans had a garrison there. <div eID="gen19040" type="x-p"/>
entries.d7da1a9cffd2de10d6915d3897851804b1267e01: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10648"/><div sID="gen19041" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10648"/><hi type="bold">19. he--</hi>Nebuchadnezzar, or Nebuzara-dan; the name would at once suggest itself to the minds of the hearers (<reference osisRef="Jer.48.40">Jr 48:40</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.46.18">46:18</reference>).<div eID="gen19041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19042" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">swelling--</hi>as a lion which the overflow of the Jordan forced out of his lair on the banks, to ascend the neighboring heights [Calvin]. See as to the translation, "pride of the Jordan," see on <reference osisRef="Jer.12.5">Jr 12:5</reference>.<div eID="gen19042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19043" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">habitation of ... strong--</hi>the fastnesses of Idumea (compare <reference osisRef="Num.24.21">Nu 24:21</reference>). Maurer translates, "An ever verdant (literally, 'perennial') pasturage," that is, Idumea heretofore having enjoyed uninterrupted tranquillity; so in <reference osisRef="Jer.49.20">Jr 49:20</reference> the image is retained, the Idumeans being compared to "a flock," and their king to "a shepherd," in this verse, and the enemy to "a lion" (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.50.17-Jer.50.19">Jr 50:17-19</reference>). English Version accords more with the Hebrew.<div eID="gen19043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19044" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">suddenly--</hi>"in the twinkling of an eye," as the Hebrew implies.<div eID="gen19044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19045" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">him ... her--</hi>I will make Nebuzara-dan enter Idumea, and then, having in the twinkling of an eye effected the conquest, go away speedily: elsewhere. Instead of "but," translate, "for." Grotius translates, "run upon her," or "to her," instead of "run away from her." Maurer understands it, "I will make him (the Idumean) run away from her" (that is, from his own land); the similar change of reference of the pronouns (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.44">Jr 50:44</reference>) favors this.<div eID="gen19045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19046" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">who is a chosen man, &c.--</hi>God calls the choicest warriors to Him, to set "over" the work of devastating Idumea. God will surely execute His purpose, for He can call forth from all sides the agents He chooses.<div eID="gen19046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19047" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">who is like me?--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Exod.15.11">Ex 15:11</reference>).<div eID="gen19047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19048" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">who will appoint me the time?--</hi>namely, for entering into a trial in judgment with Me (see Margin). Image from law courts (<reference osisRef="Job.9.19">Job 9:19</reference>).<div eID="gen19048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19049" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shepherd--</hi>leader of the Idumeans; following up the previous image, "a lion"; no Idumean shepherd shall withstand the lion sent by Jehovah (<reference osisRef="Job.41.10">Job 41:10</reference>), or save the Idumean flock. <div eID="gen19049" type="x-p"/>
entries.01afccba7c7c779fe65f0724e7a3a1a98f84de53: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10649"/><div sID="gen19050" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10649"/><hi type="bold">20. least of the flock--</hi>the weakest and humblest of the Chaldean host. Compare <reference osisRef="Jer.6.3">Jr 6:3</reference>, where the hostile leaders and their hosts are called "shepherds and their flocks."<div eID="gen19050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19051" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">draw ... out--</hi>"shall drag them away captive" [Grotius]; shall drag them to and fro, as a lion (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.19">Jr 49:19</reference>) does feeble sheep [Maurer].<div eID="gen19051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19052" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with them--</hi>that is, the habitation which they possess. <div eID="gen19052" type="x-p"/>
entries.0cc153b9c0498e1589f8d3e61674867f0c1ebb84: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10650"/><div sID="gen19053" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10650"/><hi type="bold">21. was heard in--</hi>that is, shall be heard at.<div eID="gen19053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19054" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Red Sea--</hi>a considerable distance from Idumea; though the district at the Elantic bay of the Red Sea originally belonged to Idumea, and the sea itself was called from Edom, that is, "red" (<reference osisRef="Gen.25.30">Ge 25:30</reference>, Margin). Others translate, "the weedy sea" (Margin), and derive the name, "Red Sea," from its red weeds; the former view is preferable. <div eID="gen19054" type="x-p"/>
entries.31b306abc23ba04c4dae916d6dc4f3c628452094: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10651"/><div sID="gen19055" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10651"/>22. (Compare <reference osisRef="Jer.48.40">Jr 48:40</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.41">41</reference>).<div eID="gen19055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19056" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Bozrah--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Jer.48.24">Jr 48:24</reference>). <div eID="gen19056" type="x-p"/>
entries.6023694db1a693a4ca131cfc5d41dfbb616ab3d7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10652"/><div sID="gen19057" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10652"/>23. Prophecy as to Damascus, &c. (<reference osisRef="Isa.17.1">Is 17:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.10.9">10:9</reference>). The kingdom of Damascus was destroyed by Assyria, but the city revived, and it is as to the latter Jeremiah now prophesies. The fulfilment was probably about five years after the destruction of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar [Josephus, Antiquities, 10.9,7].<div eID="gen19057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19058" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Hamath is confounded--</hi>at the tidings of the overthrow of the neighboring Damascus.<div eID="gen19058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19059" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">on the sea--</hi>that is, at the sea; the dwellers there are alarmed. Other manuscripts read, "like the sea." "There is anxiety (restless) as is the sea: they cannot quiet it," that is, it cannot be quieted (<reference osisRef="Isa.57.20">Is 57:20</reference>).<div eID="gen19059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19060" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">it--</hi>Whatever dwellers are there "cannot be quiet." <div eID="gen19060" type="x-p"/>
entries.1f2b840ac06f7d0d9b6a54f57517a92bc4bd7f80: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10653"/><div sID="gen19061" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10653"/><hi type="bold">25. city of praise--</hi>The prophet, in the person of a citizen of Damascus deploring its calamity, calls it "the city of praise," that is, celebrated with praises everywhere for its beauty (<reference osisRef="Jer.33.9">Jr 33:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.51.41">51:41</reference>). "How is it possible that such a city has not been left whole--has not been spared by the foe?" Compare left, <reference osisRef="Luke.17.35">Lu 17:35</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.17.36">36</reference>. So Israel "left" standing some of the Canaanite cities (<reference osisRef="Josh.11.13">Jos 11:13</reference>).<div eID="gen19061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19062" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of my joy--</hi>that is, in which I delighted. <div eID="gen19062" type="x-p"/>
entries.2c034228212ee720e9df69637cdd66bab0f18aeb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10654"/><div sID="gen19063" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10654"/><hi type="bold">26. Therefore--</hi>that is, Since Damascus is doomed to fall, therefore, &c. <div eID="gen19063" type="x-p"/>
entries.b5893f69baf2e67c28989cfb0acae8cb68e1d384: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10655"/><div sID="gen19064" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10655"/><hi type="bold">27. palaces of Ben-hadad--</hi>that palace from which so many evils and such cruelty to Israel emanated; thus implying the cause of Damascus' overthrow. Not the Ben-hadad of <reference osisRef="2Kgs.13.3">2Ki 13:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.1.4">Am 1:4</reference>; it was a common name of the Syrian kings (compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.18">1Ki 15:18</reference>; meaning "son of Hadad," the idol). <div eID="gen19064" type="x-p"/>
entries.81db09d7fdfaa9e1af4ef4d4935bb5c87f48e7ea: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10656"/><div sID="gen19065" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10656"/><hi type="bold">28. Kedar--</hi>son of Ishmael (<reference osisRef="Gen.25.13">Ge 25:13</reference>). The Kedarenes led a wandering predatory life in Arabia-Petræa, as the Bedouin Arabs (<reference osisRef="2Chr.21.16">2Ch 21:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.21.17">17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.120.5">Psa 120:5</reference>). Kedar means "blackness" (<reference osisRef="Song.1.5">So 1:5</reference>).<div eID="gen19065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19066" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Hazor--</hi>not the city in Palestine, but a district in Arabia-Petræa. "Kingdoms" refer to the several combinations of clans, each under its own sheik.<div eID="gen19066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19067" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">men of the east--</hi>Kedar and Hazor were east of Judea (<reference osisRef="Judg.6.3">Jud 6:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.1.3">Job 1:3</reference>). <div eID="gen19067" type="x-p"/>
entries.08603c38b4a84ca4a90da85e227a4020c5ac607c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10657"/><div sID="gen19068" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10657"/><hi type="bold">29. tents--</hi>in which they dwelt, from which they are called Scenites, that is, tent dwellers.<div eID="gen19068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19069" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">curtains--</hi>namely, with which the tents were covered (<reference osisRef="Jer.4.20">Jr 4:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.10.20">10:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.104.2">Psa 104:2</reference>).<div eID="gen19069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19070" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they shall cry unto them, Fear, &c.--</hi>The foe, on crying, Fear ..., shall discomfit them (the Kedarenes) by their mere cry. <div eID="gen19070" type="x-p"/>
entries.db036490a187eba29734cc0ae4381c8f944843f0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10658"/><div sID="gen19071" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10658"/>30. (See on <reference osisRef="Jer.49.8">Jr 49:8</reference>). No conqueror would venture to follow them into the desert. <div eID="gen19071" type="x-p"/>
entries.b8fe49bdb1707a0fced750f03dcf5da525624171: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10659"/><div sID="gen19072" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10659"/><hi type="bold">31. wealthy--</hi>rather, "tranquil" (<reference osisRef="1Chr.4.40">1Ch 4:40</reference>).<div eID="gen19072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19073" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neither gates nor bars--</hi>The Arabs, lying out of the track of the contending powers of Asia and Africa, took no measures of defense and had neither walled cities nor gates (<reference osisRef="Ezek.38.11">Eze 38:11</reference>). They thought their scanty resources and wilderness position would tempt no foe.<div eID="gen19073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19074" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">alone--</hi>separated from other nations, without allies; and from one another scattered asunder. So as to Israel's isolation (<reference osisRef="Num.23.9">Nu 23:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.33.28">De 33:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.7.14">Mi 7:14</reference>). <div eID="gen19074" type="x-p"/>
entries.58ed6c362a175852b6d3f0bfd46650d657cbacef: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10660"/><div sID="gen19075" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10660"/><hi type="bold">32. camels--</hi>their chief possessions; not fields or vineyards.<div eID="gen19075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19076" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in utmost ... corners--</hi>who seemed least likely to be dispersed. Or else, "having the hair shaven (or clipped) in angles" (<reference osisRef="Jer.9.26">Jr 9:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.25.23">25:23</reference>) [Grotius].<div eID="gen19076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19077" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">calamity from all sides--</hi>which will force even those in "corners" to "scatter" themselves. <div eID="gen19077" type="x-p"/>
entries.f49c82fb8c3b060a24daf68e4bcb95c837ae4b88: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10661"/><div sID="gen19078" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10661"/>33. (Mal 1:3). <div eID="gen19078" type="x-p"/>
entries.fc0e7ad3277c4911a4c6356d319e36963de4d1b4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10662"/><div sID="gen19079" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10662"/><hi type="bold">34. Elam--</hi>part of Susiana, west of Persia proper, but used to designate Persia in general. Elam proper, or Elymais, nearer Judea than Persia, is probably here meant; it had helped Nebuchadnezzar against Judea; hence its punishment. It may have been idolatrous, whereas Persia proper was mainly monotheistic. <div eID="gen19079" type="x-p"/>
entries.809d4a85d461b52356b61594c73e871841e02c8d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10663"/><div sID="gen19080" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10663"/><hi type="bold">35. bow--</hi>Elam was famed for its bowmen (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.6">Is 22:6</reference>).<div eID="gen19080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19081" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">chief of their might--</hi>in opposition to "bow," that is, bowmen, who constituted their main strength. <div eID="gen19081" type="x-p"/>
entries.73ada3d6aea600b8e34fdc414a0f0f896df32823: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10664"/><div sID="gen19082" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10664"/><hi type="bold">36. four winds, &c.--</hi>Nebuchadnezzar's army containing soldiers from the four quarters. <div eID="gen19082" type="x-p"/>
entries.a55b8dd5ae1538341ba77575f7eaaa9cb9bdb43e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10665"/><div sID="gen19083" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10665"/><hi type="bold">37. consumed--</hi>as a distinct nation (<reference osisRef="Dan.8.2-Dan.8.27">Da 8:2-27</reference>). Fulfilled under Alexander and his successors. <div eID="gen19083" type="x-p"/>
entries.59a7f18a3461494fdbaa0a3b4862b11e4bf53bb1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10666"/><div sID="gen19084" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10666"/>38. I will show Myself King by My judgments there, as though My tribunal were erected there. The throne of Cyrus, God's instrument, set up over Media, of which Elam was a part, may be meant [Grotius]; or rather, that of Nebuchadnezzar (<reference osisRef="Jer.43.10">Jr 43:10</reference>). Then the restoration of Elam (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.39">Jr 49:39</reference>) will refer partly to that which took place on the reduction of Babylon by Cyrus, prince of Persia and Media. <div eID="gen19084" type="x-p"/>
entries.ebe3acf12cc21794d9bfa22a1f2e9f8d65e3eb74: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10667"/><div sID="gen19085" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10667"/><hi type="bold">39. latter days--</hi>The full restoration belongs to gospel times. Elamites were among the first who heard and accepted it (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.9">Ac 2:9</reference>). <chapter eID="Jer.49"/>
